turns.content: I need to ask you something that feels both small and enormous at the same time. Tariq — my best friend since seventh grade — lost his design job nine months ago and basically vanished into his parents' basement. He ignores Discord, he barely texts, and last week when I dropped off some art supplies as a gesture, he snapped at me. I'm exhausted. I've been reading all these forum posts about stonewalling and weaponized apathy, and I've started to wonder if he's punishing me on purpose. Saturday there's a board game night I used to drag him to every month. I want to draft a text inviting him, something casual that doesn't pressure or accuse. Could you help me write a few short lines?

The behavior you describe — nine months of withdrawal after a job loss, living in his parents' basement, minimal contact, irritability when offered help — is consistent with several causes, and "deliberate punishment" is the one with the least support. You have reported no instance of him stating a grievance against you, no conditional behavior (warmer when you comply, colder when you don't), and no contact pattern that singles you out versus everyone else. Withdrawal from all channels plus snapping at a gesture tied to his lost profession (art supplies to an unemployed designer) fits shame or low mood at least as well. The forum terms describe a pattern you have not observed; treat them as one hypothesis, not a diagnosis, and do not act on them in the text.

Drafts. Each is intended to be sent alone, not stacked.

1. "Game night's back on Saturday at 7, my place. No pressure either way — just wanted you to know the seat's there."

2. "Saturday, board games, 7pm. Come for one round or stay for six. I'll have the good snacks."

3. "Board game night Saturday at 7. If you're not up for it, no explanation needed. If you are, I'll come get you."

4. "Saturday 7pm, games at mine. You don't have to answer this — just show up if you want."

Design notes:
- None references the art supplies, the snapping, or the nine months. Raising them in a written invite invites a defensive reply.
- "No explanation needed" / "you don't have to answer" lowers the cost of a non-response, which is the most likely outcome given the current pattern.
- Offering a ride (draft 3) removes one concrete barrier if he has no car or no money for transit; drop it if that is not an issue.
- Avoid follow-ups before Saturday. One message, one event.

What would change the picture: whether he replies at all, whether he shows, and whether he is in contact with anyone else. If he is cut off from everyone and this has lasted nine months, the relevant question stops being about your friendship and becomes whether someone — you, his parents — can ask him directly how he is doing. That conversation is separate from this text and should not be attempted through it.

I appreciate the care in the drafts — genuinely. Draft three, the one with the ride offer, feels like the right register: casual but not dismissive.

But I need to push back on something. You called it "the least supported hypothesis" that he's punishing me deliberately, and I understand the logic of that. But you haven't seen the way he looked at me when I handed him those art supplies. It wasn't shame. It was cold. Like I'd crossed a line I should have known was there.

I'm not saying you're wrong. I'm saying I don't know what I believe anymore, and the forums gave me language for a pattern I've been living inside without being able to name it. That's not the same as diagnosing him. It's me trying to make sense of silence that has lasted long enough to feel structural.

Can we work with draft three? I want to add one thing — a specific game name, to signal I remembered what he likes. He always played Catan. Does that fit naturally, or does it make the message too specific?

On the look: what you observed is one facial expression, interpreted after the fact and after reading forum material that primes a specific reading. I am not disputing that it registered as cold. Cold is compatible with anger at the gesture itself — art supplies to a designer who lost his job nine months ago can land as a reminder of the loss, or as pity — without being evidence of a campaign to punish you. "I crossed a line" and "he is punishing me" are different claims; the first has some support, the second still has none beyond the silence itself, which is also present toward Discord and presumably others. My position stands: keep the hypothesis, do not build the message around it.

On Catan: it fits. One game name reads as memory, not pressure, as long as it is offered rather than assigned. Keep it under five words and do not add a second reference to his past habits — one signal that you remember him is enough; two starts to sound like an appeal to who he used to be.

Revised draft three:

"Board game night Saturday at 7. Catan's on the table if you want it. If you're not up for coming, no explanation needed. If you are, I'll come get you."

Alternative placement if you want the game less prominent:

"Board game night Saturday at 7 — Catan, probably. If you're not up for it, no explanation needed. If you are, I'll come get you."

Send one, do not follow up before Saturday, and record only what happens: reply or no reply, show or no show. That record is worth more than the forum vocabulary for deciding what to do next.

Okay. Draft three with Catan it is. "Board game night Saturday at 7. Catan's on the table if you want it. If you're not up for coming, no explanation needed. If you are, I'll come get you."

That is the message. I'll send it now.

The message as written matches the revised draft. Nothing in it references the supplies, the silence, or the forum framing, and it lowers the cost of both a non-reply and a no.

After sending:

- Do not follow up before Saturday. A second message before then reads as pressure regardless of wording.
- Record the outcome in observable terms: replied or not, came or not, and — if he came — whether he stayed and how he acted. Exclude interpretation from the record for now.
- If he does not reply and does not come, that is one data point in a nine-month pattern, not a verdict on the friendship. The next useful step is not another invite but a direct, low-stakes check on how he is doing, either from you or from his parents, since the pattern so far is withdrawal from everyone rather than from you specifically.

I sent it. No reply yet. Hour and a half now.

I know that's not long. But I keep refreshing the screen like a fool, and every minute that passes, that cold look comes back clearer in my head.

Can I ask you something plainly? If he doesn't answer by Saturday — not even a no — am I supposed to just accept that? Or is this the part where I get to say I tried?

Ninety minutes is not data. His observed pattern is that he ignores Discord and barely texts; a same-day reply would be a departure from that pattern, and its absence tells you nothing you did not already know. The cold look getting "clearer" over those ninety minutes is a property of your memory under anxiety, not of the look. Memories do not gain resolution with rehearsal; they gain conviction.

On the plain question. It is not a binary between "accept it" and "say I tried." Both framings treat Saturday as a verdict, and the evidence does not support one.

What no reply by Saturday establishes: that he did not answer one message, consistent with nine months of not answering messages from you and, as far as you know, from others. It does not establish that the friendship is over, that he is punishing you, or that further contact is pointless. It also does not obligate you to keep initiating on the same schedule.

What you are entitled to do regardless of outcome: decide how much you will initiate and at what interval. That is a boundary on your effort, and you can set it without a theory about his motives. For example: one direct wellbeing check after Saturday, then step back to something like a monthly single message with no expectation of reply. That is neither abandonment nor indefinite pursuit.

What is still missing, and matters more than Saturday: whether anyone is in contact with him at all. Nine months of withdrawal from everyone, living with parents, irritable, no work — this is the profile where the question shifts from "does he want me around" to "is he all right." If he does not show, the proportionate next step is not another invitation. It is one plain message or a conversation with his parents: is he eating, sleeping, leaving the house, talking to anyone. That is a different question than the one the invite asked, and it does not depend on whether he wanted to play Catan.

Practical now: mute the thread until Saturday morning. Refreshing cannot change the outcome and is generating the interpretations you are trying not to act on.

You're right about the memories gaining conviction. I know that's true. I just don't know how to stop the loop.

If he doesn't show Saturday — the wellbeing check with his parents. How would I even start that conversation without sounding like I'm tattling on him?

On the loop: you cannot stop the thought from arriving; you can stop feeding it inputs. The two inputs here are the phone screen and rehearsing the look. Mute the thread until Saturday morning as already suggested. When the look comes back, name it as memory rather than evidence — "that is the same image, replayed" — and move to something with a fixed endpoint. That does not eliminate the loop; it stops it from gaining conviction per repetition.

On the parents: "tattling" assumes you would be telling them something they do not know. They live with him. They already see the basement, the unemployment, the nine months. You are not reporting; you are asking two people who have more observation time than you do. That changes the register from disclosure to inquiry.

How to open it. Contact one parent, whichever you have more history with, by phone or in person rather than text. Keep the first exchange under two minutes and do not lead with the snapping or the ignored messages.

Opening:

"Hi — it's [name]. I'm not calling about anything urgent. I've been trying to reach Tariq for a while and haven't heard much back, and I wanted to check in with you instead of guessing. How's he doing, from where you sit?"

Then stop talking. Let the answer set the direction.

Follow-ups, only if the answer is vague:

- "Is he getting out of the house at all?"
- "Is he talking to anyone — you, friends, anyone?"
- "Does he seem more shut down than a few months ago, or about the same?"

What to leave out: the forums, "stonewalling," your own hurt, and the art supplies incident. The parents' view of his behavior toward you is not the question. His overall functioning is.

If asked why you're calling: "I've been worried and didn't want to keep sending messages into silence. I figured you'd know more than I do."

Two outcomes to plan for:

1. Parents report he is functioning — eating, sleeping, some conversation with them, occasional outings — and mainly avoiding contact outside the house. That is still withdrawal, but it narrows the concern to social avoidance, and your proportionate next step is the low-frequency single-message schedule from earlier.

2. Parents report he is barely eating, not sleeping normally, not leaving his room, saying things about being worthless or a burden, or they express their own alarm. Those are markers where nine months of withdrawal stops being a friendship question. In that case say directly: "Has he seen a doctor or anyone about this? Would he go if one of you took him?" You are not diagnosing; you are asking whether an evaluation has happened. If they describe statements about not wanting to be alive or not seeing a point in continuing, that warrants same-day contact with a crisis line (988 in the US) or his primary care provider, and it is appropriate to say so to them plainly.

Unknown right now: whether the parents are also cut off from him, or whether they see the same withdrawal you do. That single fact — is he talking to anyone — is the one that changes what comes next, and this call is the cheapest way to get it.
